If the Redstone was the cautious step, the Atlas was the leap. It was America's first intercontinental missile, and it reached orbital speed by being audaciously, almost alarmingly light: its skin was so thin that the rocket had to be kept pressurised like a balloon just to stand up without crumpling. Man-rating that — trusting a person to a missile that would collapse if you let the pressure drop — was the hard call that separated Mercury's suborbital half from its orbital one. Every American orbital flight of the program rode this thin steel balloon, and it is why Glenn, Carpenter, Schirra, and Cooper circled the Earth while Shepard and Grissom only touched the edge of it.

Atlas LV-3B was Convair's orbital launcher that lifted Mercury astronauts to orbit on four flights (Mercury-Atlas 6 through 9) between February 1962 and May 1963. The thin-skinned booster — so light it required pressurization to stand upright — proved that a ballistic missile could be man-rated. Retired after the Mercury program.
First American to orbit the Earth
Repeated Glenn's 3-orbit profile; overshot landing target by 400 km
First textbook Mercury flight — 6 orbits; double Glenn / Carpenter duration
Last solo American orbital flight; 22 orbits / 34 hours
Cape Canaveral Mercury-Atlas pad — launched all 4 orbital Mercury flights (Glenn / Carpenter / Schirra / Cooper, 1962-1963)
First US human-rated launcher — variant of the Army's Redstone IRBM. Launched Freedom 7 (1961-05-05) and Liberty Bell 7 (1961-07-21)
Lifted Apollo 7, Skylab crews, and ASTP
1970s NASA outer-planet workhorse — Pioneer 10/11, Helios 1/2, Mariner 9/10, Pioneer Venus
